growth_story.headline: South Africa's income per person climbed in 2000–2008, then stalled as power cuts spread and mines and exports faded; it is now back at its 2006 level.
growth_story.arc: Income per person drifted down in the 1990s, at -0.3 percent a year. From 2000 to 2008 it grew 3.1 percent a year. The 2009 global crisis cut it by 2.7 percent, and from 2009 to 2025 it averaged -0.3 percent a year: it peaked in 2013 and is now 7.4 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 2006. The sources tie this long stall to power cuts that began in 2007 and worsened, and to fading mines, factories and exports; investment also fell, from 21.6 percent of GDP in 2008 to 13.9 in 2025. The pandemic drop of 7.7 percent in 2020 was only partly made up by 3.3 percent growth in 2021, so over 2016–2025 income per person fell 0.6 percent a year, against 1.3 in the decade before. Recent reforms in power, rail and ports have lifted total output a little, but not yet income per person.

threads.title: Power cuts from 2007
threads.text: From 2007 Eskom could not meet peak demand for electricity and began rolling power cuts, which grew worse in the years after. The Growth Lab ties a large part of South Africa's growth slowdown to the collapse of its utilities.

citations.title: Growth Through Inclusion in South Africa
citations.quote: Beginning in 2007, peak demand for electricity began to outstrip supply, and Eskom started to use load-shedding to balance the system.

citations.title: Growth Through Inclusion in South Africa
citations.quote: Since then, the electricity issue has only worsened with load-shedding intensifying and electricity prices rising.

citations.title: Growth Through Inclusion in South Africa
citations.quote: The collapse of utilities overall can explain around 40% of South Africa’s growth slowdown even before the recent escalation of the crisis

threads.title: Mines, factories and exports faded
threads.text: Mining began to weaken before 2008, even while world prices were still strong, and manufacturing has shed jobs since 2008. Export volumes stalled too, so the slowdown was more than a fall in commodity prices.

citations.title: Growth Through Inclusion in South Africa
citations.quote: The weakening of mining began before 2008 — despite global commodity prices remaining strong for several years after

citations.title: Growth Through Inclusion in South Africa
citations.quote: Manufacturing shed jobs since 2008 at a pace well beyond what global trends of “premature deindustrialization” can explain

citations.title: Growth Through Inclusion in South Africa
citations.quote: This change cannot be explained by a decline in commodity prices alone because export volumes also stagnated.

threads.title: Reform of power, rail, ports
threads.text: Under Operation Vulindlela, rules were changed to deepen competition in power, rail and telecoms. The World Bank reports far fewer power cuts, more rail freight and smoother ports, while the IMF judges the pace of reform still too slow for lasting growth and jobs.

citations.title: New World Bank Report Highlights Four Pathways to Spur Job Creation and Inclusive Growth in South Africa
citations.quote: the first phase of Operation Vulindlela, which among its key interventions was reforms to regulation that deepened competition in sectors like electricity, rail and telecoms

citations.title: South Africa (country overview)
citations.quote: Performance at key state-owned enterprises is improving, with a substantial reduction in load-shedding, increased rail freight, and more efficient port operations.

citations.title: South Africa: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2025 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Assessment: pace of reforms not yet commensurate with needs to generate sustainable growth and jobs.

threads.title: Jobs in a split economy
threads.text: Unemployment was 32.3 percent in 2025 and rose further in 2026, and the World Bank says growth has been too weak to create enough jobs. It describes two economies side by side, one with high levels of development and productivity and one with much lower levels.

citations.title: South Africa (country overview)
citations.quote: The unemployment rate rose to 33.6% in Q2 of 2026, leaving 8.5 million people unemployed.

citations.title: South Africa (country overview)
citations.quote: Economic growth has been insufficient to create enough jobs or significantly reduce poverty.

citations.title: South Africa (country overview)
citations.quote: South Africa remains a dual economy - one with high levels of development, technology, and productivity, and one with much lower levels

since_last_year.text: Total output picked up in 2025, which the IMF credits to strong household spending and the World Bank to reforms beginning to show results. The economy then shrank in the second quarter of 2026 as oil prices rose and demand weakened.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with South Africa
citations.quote: Economic activity picked up in 2025, with growth estimated at 1.3 percent, supported by robust private consumption.

citations.title: South Africa (country overview)
citations.quote: Economic growth increased from 0.5% in 2024 to 1.1% in 2025, as structural reforms began to yield results.

citations.title: South Africa (country overview)
citations.quote: After expanding by 0.5% in Q1 of 2026, the economy contracted by 0.2% in Q2 as higher oil prices and weaker demand weighed on activity.

growth_story.tension: The IMF and World Bank describe 2025 as a year when growth picked up, but in the data income per person was flat in 2025: the gain in total output was roughly matched by population growth.
